CALIFORNIA SUBDIVIDED LANDS LAW — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme Land Development, LLC · Jordan Alex Lee

DECLARATION OF SUBDIVISION, OWNER/SUBDIVIDER, AND PROSPECTIVE PURCHASER
This information sheet describes California's Subdivided Lands Law (Bus. & Prof. Code § 11000 et seq., within the Business and Professions Code's Real Estate division), a statutory scheme administered by the California Department of Real Estate that is separate from, and imposes different requirements than, the Subdivision Map Act's local-government map-approval process. It describes this body of law as it relates to land described as: Sunrise Meadows Subdivision, Lots 1–24, Placer County, California, offered by Acme Land Development, LLC as owner or subdivider, to prospective purchaser Jordan Alex Lee. As described in the clauses below, this law can require an owner or subdivider to obtain a public report from the Department of Real Estate before offering qualifying subdivided lands for sale or lease, and can require delivery of that report to a prospective purchaser before a binding contract is signed. This declaration states these facts about the parties and the property; it does not itself determine whether this specific offering meets the statutory definition of "subdivided lands," whether a public report has been issued or is required for it, or whether any statutory exemption applies.

STATUTORY DEFINITION OF "SUBDIVIDED LANDS": THE FIVE-OR-MORE-LOT THRESHOLD
California's Subdivided Lands Law defines its own core trigger in Bus. & Prof. Code § 11000(a). "Subdivided lands" and "subdivision" mean improved or unimproved land, anywhere in California, that is divided or proposed to be divided, for the purpose of sale, lease, or financing (whether immediate or future), into five or more lots or parcels. The statute carves out land sold in government-survey lots or parcels of not less than 160 acres, appearing as such on the current county assessment roll — unless that land is divided or proposed to be divided for oil and gas sale purposes, in which case the 160-acre carve-out does not apply and the land is treated as "subdivided lands." The statute also carves the leasing of apartments, offices, stores, or similar space within an apartment, industrial, or commercial building, or within a mobilehome park (as defined in Health & Safety Code § 18214), out of this chapter's coverage — except that offering a mobilehome-park tenant a lease longer than five years, as a mandatory condition of tenancy, is expressly pulled back into this chapter's coverage.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(a) “Subdivided lands” and “subdivision” refer to improved or unimproved land or lands, wherever situated within California, divided or proposed to be divided for the purpose of sale or lease or financing, whether immediate or future, into five or more lots or parcels."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 11000(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code, definition of "subdivided lands" and "subdivision" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=11000.)
  "This chapter also does not apply to the leasing of apartments, offices, stores, or similar space within an apartment building, industrial building, commercial building, or mobilehome park, as defined under Section 18214 of the Health and Safety Code, except that the offering of leases for a term in excess of five years to tenants within a mobilehome park as a mandatory requirement and prerequisite to tenancy within the mobilehome park shall be subject to the provisions of this chapter."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 11000(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code, carve-out for leasing of apartments, offices, stores, or mobilehome park space (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=11000.)
  Known gap: This clause addresses only the core five-or-more-lot definition and its two express statutory carve-outs in § 11000(a); it does not address the additional categories of interest that a separate statute, Bus. & Prof. Code § 11004.5, expressly folds into the "subdivided lands" definition (addressed in the next clause), and it does not determine whether any specific parcel configuration, government-survey designation, or lease arrangement actually meets or is excluded from this definition — that depends on facts about the specific land, survey records, and lease terms that this information sheet does not supply. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California itself defines the term for purposes of this chapter — not a claim about how any other state defines a comparable term, or that every state regulates land subdivision through a five-or-more-lot threshold; some states use different numeric thresholds or different triggering criteria entirely.

STATUTORY EXPANSION: PLANNED DEVELOPMENTS, CONDOMINIUMS, STOCK COOPERATIVES, AND SIMILAR INTERESTS
A second definitional statute, Bus. & Prof. Code § 11004.5, adds to the core § 11000 definition rather than replacing it. In addition to the provisions of § 11000, "subdivided lands" and "subdivision" also include: any planned development (as defined in § 11003) containing five or more lots; any community apartment project (as defined in § 11004) containing five or more apartments; any condominium project containing five or more condominiums (as defined in Civil Code § 783); any stock cooperative (as defined in § 11003.2) with five or more shareholders, existing or intended; and any limited-equity housing cooperative (as defined in § 11003.4). The statute separately extends coverage to accompanying memberships, rights, or privileges created in connection with those forms of development, and to interests or memberships in an owners' association (as defined in Civil Code § 4080 or § 6528) created in connection with them. The statute also states an express carve-out: time-share plans, exchange programs, incidental benefits, and short-term products regulated under the separate Vacation Ownership and Time-Share Act of 2004 (Bus. & Prof. Code § 11210 et seq.) are not "subdivisions" or "subdivided lands" under this chapter.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "In addition to the provisions of Section 11000, the reference in this code to “subdivided lands” and “subdivision” shall include all of the following:(a) Any planned development, as defined in Section 11003, containing five or more lots.(b) Any community apartment project, as defined by Section 11004, containing five or more apartments.(c) Any condominium project containing five or more condominiums, as defined in Section 783 of the Civil Code.(d) Any stock cooperative as defined in Section 11003.2, including any legal or beneficial interests therein, having or intended to have five or more shareholders.(e) Any limited-equity housing cooperative, as defined in Section 11003.4."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 11004.5(a)-(e) (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code, categories of development included within "subdivided lands" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=11004.5.)
  "Notwithstanding this section, time-share plans, exchange programs, incidental benefits, and short-term product subject to Chapter 2 (commencing with Section 11210) are not “subdivisions” or “subdivided lands” subject to this chapter."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 11004.5(g) (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code, carve-out for time-share plans and related interests (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=11004.5.)
  Known gap: This clause addresses only which categories of development or ownership interest the statute expressly folds into the "subdivided lands" definition, and the statute's express carve-out for time-share interests; it does not itself determine whether a specific planned development, condominium project, stock cooperative, or limited-equity housing cooperative meets the five-or-more-unit threshold for any of these categories, and it does not address the separate statutory public-report and disclosure requirements this corpus documents elsewhere for time-share purchases. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California itself expands its subdivided-lands definition — not a claim about how any other state defines comparable development categories.

STATUTORY DEFINITION OF "BLANKET ENCUMBRANCE"
Bus. & Prof. Code § 11013 defines a term used elsewhere in this statutory scheme to describe liens affecting more than one lot in a subdivision. A "blanket encumbrance" means a trust deed, mortgage, or any other lien or encumbrance (including a mechanics' lien), that secures or evidences payment of money and that affects either the land to be subdivided as a whole or more than one lot or parcel of subdivided land, or an agreement affecting more than one such lot or parcel under which the owner or subdivider holds the subdivision under an option, contract to sell, or trust agreement.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "For the purposes of this part, a blanket encumbrance shall be considered to mean a trust deed or mortgage or any other lien or encumbrance, mechanics’ lien or otherwise, securing or evidencing the payment of money and affecting land to be subdivided or affecting more than one lot or parcel of subdivided land, or an agreement affecting more than one such lot or parcel by which the owner or subdivider holds said subdivision under an option, contract to sell, or trust agreement."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 11013 (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code, definition of "blanket encumbrance" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=11013.)
  Known gap: This clause states only the statutory definition of "blanket encumbrance" itself; it does not address the specific statutory consequences that attach when a blanket encumbrance exists on a subdivision (for example, particular financial-arrangement showings the commissioner may require before issuing a public report), which are governed by other sections of this chapter not documented in this information sheet. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California itself defines this term — not a claim about how any other state's subdivided-land or real-estate statutes define a comparable concept.

THE PUBLIC REPORT APPLICATION REQUIREMENT: NOTICE OF INTENTION FILED WITH THE DEPARTMENT OF REAL ESTATE
Bus. & Prof. Code § 11010 requires a person who intends to offer subdivided lands within California for sale or lease to file an application for a public report with the Department of Real Estate before doing so, except as otherwise provided in subdivision (c) or elsewhere in the chapter. That application consists of a notice of intention and a completed questionnaire, on forms the department prepares. The notice of intention must contain specified categories of information about the subdivided lands and the proposed offering, including (among eighteen enumerated categories) the name and address of the owner, the name and address of the subdivider, the legal description and area of the land, and a true statement of the condition of title, including all encumbrances. Other enumerated categories in the same subdivision separately require, where applicable, a Mello-Roos special-tax notice under Civil Code § 1102.6c (a mechanism this corpus documents in a separate Residential Purchase Agreement clause), school-district statements, an airport-vicinity notice, a soils/geologic-report statement, and, where the property lies within one mile of designated farmland, a "Notice of Right to Farm" referencing Civil Code § 3482.5.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(a) Except as otherwise provided pursuant to subdivision (c) or elsewhere in this chapter, any person who intends to offer subdivided lands within this state for sale or lease shall file with the Department of Real Estate an application for a public report consisting of a notice of intention and a completed questionnaire on a form prepared by the department."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 11010(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code, requirement to file an application for a public report (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=11010.)
  "(b) The notice of intention shall contain the following information about the subdivided lands and the proposed offering:(1) The name and address of the owner.(2) The name and address of the subdivider.(3) The legal description and area of lands.(4) A true statement of the condition of the title to the land, particularly including all encumbrances thereon."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 11010(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code, first categories of required notice-of-intention content (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=11010.)
  Known gap: This clause addresses only the filing requirement and the first several categories of required notice-of-intention content; it does not reproduce or analyze all eighteen enumerated categories in § 11010(b) — several of which (the airport notice, the San Francisco Bay Conservation and Development Commission notice, and the right-to-farm notice) contain lengthy prescribed statutory text this information sheet does not quote in full — and it does not determine which categories actually apply to any specific offering, which depends on facts about that subdivision's location and characteristics. Subdivision (c)'s questionnaire-waiver authority is also not addressed here. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own application requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific offering, or that every state requires an equivalent filing.

COMMISSIONER'S EXAMINATION AND THE STATUTORY GROUNDS FOR DENYING A PUBLIC REPORT
Bus. & Prof. Code § 11018 governs what happens after a notice of intention and questionnaire are filed. The Real Estate Commissioner examines the subdivision and, unless statutory grounds for denial exist, must issue the subdivider a public report authorizing sale or lease of the lots or parcels in California; the report contains the data obtained under § 11010, plus whatever else the commissioner determines is needed to implement the article's purposes, and the commissioner may publish it. The statute enumerates nine grounds on which the commissioner may deny a public report: failure to comply with this chapter or the commissioner's regulations; a sale or lease that would misrepresent, deceive, or defraud purchasers or lessees; inability to deliver the title or interest contracted for; inadequate financial arrangements for offsite improvements; inadequate financial arrangements for community, recreational, or other included facilities; failure to show the parcels can be used for their offered purpose (and, for residential subdivisions, failure to show vehicular access and a source of potable domestic water is or will be available); failure to state the offered use and any applicable covenants or conditions in the contract or other writing; noncompliant management agreements or bylaws for common facilities; and inadequate financial arrangements for any guaranty or warranty included in the offering.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The Real Estate Commissioner shall make an examination of any subdivision, and shall, unless there are grounds for denial, issue to the subdivider a public report authorizing the sale or lease in this state of the lots or parcels within the subdivision."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 11018 (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code, commissioner's examination and duty to issue a public report (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=11018.)
  "The grounds for denial are:(a) Failure to comply with any of the provisions in this chapter or the regulations of the commissioner pertaining thereto.(b) The sale or lease would constitute misrepresentation to or deceit or fraud of the purchasers or lessees.(c) Inability to deliver title or other interest contracted for.(d) Inability to demonstrate that adequate financial arrangements have been made for all offsite improvements included in the offering.(e) Inability to demonstrate that adequate financial arrangements have been made for any community, recreational or other facilities included in the offering. (f) Failure to make a showing that the parcels can be used for the purpose for which they are offered; and in the case of a subdivision being offered for residential purposes failure to make a showing that vehicular access and a source of potable domestic water either is available or will be available.(g) Failure to provide in the contract or other writing the use or uses for which the parcels are offered, together with any covenants or conditions relative thereto.(h) Agreements or bylaws to provide for management or other services pertaining to common facilities in the offering, which fail to comply with the regulations of the commissioner.(i) Failure to demonstrate that adequate financial arrangements have been made for any guaranty or warranty included in the offering."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 11018(a)-(i) (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code, the nine enumerated grounds for denial of a public report (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=11018.)
  Known gap: This clause states the examination process and the nine enumerated denial grounds themselves; it does not address the separate procedures for amending, renewing, or suspending a public report once issued, does not address the commissioner's investigative or subpoena powers, and does not determine whether any specific ground for denial applies to a particular subdivision — that depends on facts about that offering's title, financing, and contract terms that this information sheet does not supply. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual grounds California's regulator applies — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific offering, or that every state's real-estate regulator reviews subdivision offerings against the same criteria.

REQUIREMENT TO DELIVER THE PUBLIC REPORT BEFORE A BINDING CONTRACT, AND TO MAKE IT AVAILABLE TO THE PUBLIC
Bus. & Prof. Code § 11018.1(a)-(b) imposes two distinct delivery obligations once a public report has been issued. First, the owner, subdivider, or agent must give a copy of the public report to the prospective purchaser before the purchaser executes a binding contract or agreement for the sale or lease of any lot or parcel — an obligation that extends to lots or parcels the subdivider offers after repossession — and must take a receipt from the prospective purchaser in the form the Real Estate Commissioner's regulations specify. Second, separately from that purchaser-specific delivery obligation, the owner, subdivider, or agent must give a copy of the public report to any member of the public, at any time, on oral or written request, and must post a copy of the report, with a statement that a copy is available on request, in a conspicuous place at any office where sales, leases, or offers to sell or lease lots in the subdivision are regularly made.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(a) A copy of the public report of the commissioner, when issued, shall be given to the prospective purchaser by the owner, subdivider, or agent prior to the execution of a binding contract or agreement for the sale or lease of any lot or parcel in a subdivision. The requirement of this section extends to lots or parcels offered by the subdivider after repossession. A receipt shall be taken from the prospective purchaser in a form and manner as set forth in regulations of the Real Estate Commissioner."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 11018.1(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code, requirement to deliver the public report before a binding contract (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=11018.1.)
  "(b) A copy of the public report shall be given by the owner, subdivider, or agent at any time, upon oral or written request, to any member of the public. A copy of the public report and a statement advising that a copy of the public report may be obtained from the owner, subdivider or agent at any time, upon oral or written request, shall be posted in a conspicuous place at any office where sales or leases or offers to sell or lease lots within the subdivision are regularly made."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 11018.1(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code, requirement to make the public report available to the public and post it (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=11018.1.)
  Known gap: This clause addresses only the delivery, receipt, and posting mechanics in § 11018.1(a)-(b); it does not address the additional statement a subdivider must give a purchaser when the subdivision is a common interest development (addressed in the next clause), and it does not itself confirm that a public report has been delivered, that a receipt was taken, or that posting occurred for any specific offering — those are factual questions this information sheet does not resolve. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own delivery mechanism — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific offering.

ADDITIONAL REQUIRED STATEMENT FOR COMMON INTEREST DEVELOPMENT SUBDIVISIONS
Bus. & Prof. Code § 11018.1(c) layers an additional requirement onto the public-report delivery obligation described in the preceding clause, specifically for subdivisions that are common interest developments as defined in Civil Code § 4100. At the same time the public report must be given under subdivision (a), the owner, subdivider, or agent must also give the prospective purchaser a copy of a statutory "Common Interest Development General Information" statement — prescribed statutory text describing, among other things, that the project is a common interest development, that ownership carries mandatory association membership and assessment obligations, and that governing documents (a Declaration of Restrictions/CC&Rs, articles of incorporation, and bylaws) control the purchaser's rights. The statute separately provides that failing to give this particular statement is not treated as a violation subject to Bus. & Prof. Code § 10185, a different statutory enforcement provision.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(c) At the same time that a public report is required to be given by the owner, subdivider, or agent pursuant to subdivision (a) with respect to a common interest development, as defined, in Section 4100 of the Civil Code, the owner, subdivider, or agent shall give the prospective purchaser a copy of the following statement: “Common Interest Development General Information"
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 11018.1(c) (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code, requirement to give a Common Interest Development General Information statement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=11018.1.)
  "Failure to provide the statement in accordance with this subdivision shall not be deemed a violation subject to Section 10185."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 11018.1(c) (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code, non-delivery of this statement not a violation subject to § 10185 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=11018.1.)
  Known gap: This clause states that the statement is required and that its non-delivery is carved out from § 10185 enforcement; it does not quote the full prescribed statement text (which runs to several paragraphs), does not address what other enforcement avenue, if any, applies to a failure to give this specific statement, and does not address the separate Davis-Stirling Common Interest Development disclosure obligations this corpus documents elsewhere for HOA/CC&R disclosures generally, which arise under different statutes at different points in a CID transaction. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own additional CID-specific requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific offering.

CRIMINAL PENALTIES FOR VIOLATING ENUMERATED PROVISIONS OF THE SUBDIVIDED LANDS LAW
Bus. & Prof. Code § 11023 attaches criminal exposure to violations of a specific, enumerated list of sections within this chapter: §§ 11010, 11010.1, 11010.8, 11013.1, 11013.2, 11013.4, 11018.2, 11018.7, 11018.9, 11018.10, 11018.11, 11019, and 11022. A violation of any of those enumerated sections is a public offense punishable by a fine not exceeding $10,000, or imprisonment under Penal Code § 1170(h) or in a county jail not exceeding one year, or both the fine and imprisonment.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Any person who violates Section 11010, 11010.1, 11010.8, 11013.1, 11013.2, 11013.4, 11018.2, 11018.7, 11018.9, 11018.10, 11018.11, 11019, or 11022 is guilty of a public offense punishable by a fine not exceeding ten thousand dollars ($10,000) or by imprisonment pursuant to subdivision (h) of Section 1170 of the Penal Code, or in a county jail not exceeding one year, or by both that fine and imprisonment."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 11023 (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code, criminal penalty for violating enumerated sections of the Subdivided Lands Law (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=11023.)
  Known gap: The enumerated list in § 11023 does not include every section this information sheet describes: it lists § 11010 (the notice-of-intention filing requirement) but does not list § 11018 (the commissioner's examination and public-report issuance) or § 11018.1 (delivery of the report to a purchaser or the public) among the sections whose violation triggers this specific criminal penalty — meaning this statute's own text does not extend this particular sanction to every obligation this information sheet describes, and this clause does not address what other penalty, if any, attaches to a violation of a section not on this list. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual criminal exposure and the actual enumerated sections California's own text lists — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific violation, or that every state enforces comparable subdivided-lands requirements through criminal penalties.

REQUIRED CONTENTS OF A SUBDIVISION SALES CONTRACT
Bus. & Prof. Code § 11200 imposes a content requirement on the sales contract itself for a subdivision within this chapter's definition. Every sales contract for the purchase of real property in such a subdivision must clearly set forth: the legal description of the property, the encumbrances outstanding as of the date of the sales contract, and the terms of the contract.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Every sales contract relating to the purchase of real property in a subdivision as defined in this chapter shall clearly set forth the legal description of the property, of the encumbrances outstanding at the date of the sales contract, and the terms of the contract."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 11200 (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code, required contents of a subdivision sales contract (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=11200.)
  Known gap: This clause states only this specific content requirement for the sales contract; it does not address the separate notice-of-intention content requirements for the public-report application (documented in an earlier clause), does not specify a required format for stating the legal description, encumbrances, or terms, and does not determine whether a specific sales contract's actual content satisfies this requirement — that depends on the contract's own text, which this information sheet does not supply. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own sales-contract content requirement for subdivided lands — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific sales contract.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT OF REVIEW
This information sheet, describing California's Subdivided Lands Law as it relates to the offering described above involving Acme Land Development, LLC and Jordan Alex Lee, has been reviewed by the parties named below. This acknowledgment confirms only that this information sheet was reviewed. It is not the public report the Department of Real Estate issues under Bus. & Prof. Code § 11018, it does not satisfy the receipt requirement Bus. & Prof. Code § 11018.1(a) separately imposes for delivery of that report, and it is not the Common Interest Development General Information statement Bus. & Prof. Code § 11018.1(c) separately requires for a common interest development subdivision; none of those statutory documents or requirements is satisfied by this signature block, and each must be completed separately if California law requires it for this offering.

expectedJSON.body: Bus. & Prof. Code § 11013 defines a term used elsewhere in this statutory scheme to describe liens affecting more than one lot in a subdivision. A "blanket encumbrance" means a trust deed, mortgage, or any other lien or encumbrance (including a mechanics' lien), that secures or evidences payment of money and that affects either the land to be subdivided as a whole or more than one lot or parcel of subdivided land, or an agreement affecting more than one such lot or parcel under which the owner or subdivider holds the subdivision under an option, contract to sell, or trust agreement.

expectedJSON.body: Bus. & Prof. Code § 11010 requires a person who intends to offer subdivided lands within California for sale or lease to file an application for a public report with the Department of Real Estate before doing so, except as otherwise provided in subdivision (c) or elsewhere in the chapter. That application consists of a notice of intention and a completed questionnaire, on forms the department prepares. The notice of intention must contain specified categories of information about the subdivided lands and the proposed offering, including (among eighteen enumerated categories) the name and address of the owner, the name and address of the subdivider, the legal description and area of the land, and a true statement of the condition of title, including all encumbrances. Other enumerated categories in the same subdivision separately require, where applicable, a Mello-Roos special-tax notice under Civil Code § 1102.6c (a mechanism this corpus documents in a separate Residential Purchase Agreement clause), school-district statements, an airport-vicinity notice, a soils/geologic-report statement, and, where the property lies within one mile of designated farmland, a "Notice of Right to Farm" referencing Civil Code § 3482.5.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 11010(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code, requirement to file an application for a public report
citations.quote: (a) Except as otherwise provided pursuant to subdivision (c) or elsewhere in this chapter, any person who intends to offer subdivided lands within this state for sale or lease shall file with the Department of Real Estate an application for a public report consisting of a notice of intention and a completed questionnaire on a form prepared by the department.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 11010(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code, first categories of required notice-of-intention content
citations.quote: (b) The notice of intention shall contain the following information about the subdivided lands and the proposed offering:(1) The name and address of the owner.(2) The name and address of the subdivider.(3) The legal description and area of lands.(4) A true statement of the condition of the title to the land, particularly including all encumbrances thereon.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause addresses only the filing requirement and the first several categories of required notice-of-intention content; it does not reproduce or analyze all eighteen enumerated categories in § 11010(b) — several of which (the airport notice, the San Francisco Bay Conservation and Development Commission notice, and the right-to-farm notice) contain lengthy prescribed statutory text this information sheet does not quote in full — and it does not determine which categories actually apply to any specific offering, which depends on facts about that subdivision's location and characteristics. Subdivision (c)'s questionnaire-waiver authority is also not addressed here. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own application requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific offering, or that every state requires an equivalent filing.

expectedJSON.body: Bus. & Prof. Code § 11018 governs what happens after a notice of intention and questionnaire are filed. The Real Estate Commissioner examines the subdivision and, unless statutory grounds for denial exist, must issue the subdivider a public report authorizing sale or lease of the lots or parcels in California; the report contains the data obtained under § 11010, plus whatever else the commissioner determines is needed to implement the article's purposes, and the commissioner may publish it. The statute enumerates nine grounds on which the commissioner may deny a public report: failure to comply with this chapter or the commissioner's regulations; a sale or lease that would misrepresent, deceive, or defraud purchasers or lessees; inability to deliver the title or interest contracted for; inadequate financial arrangements for offsite improvements; inadequate financial arrangements for community, recreational, or other included facilities; failure to show the parcels can be used for their offered purpose (and, for residential subdivisions, failure to show vehicular access and a source of potable domestic water is or will be available); failure to state the offered use and any applicable covenants or conditions in the contract or other writing; noncompliant management agreements or bylaws for common facilities; and inadequate financial arrangements for any guaranty or warranty included in the offering.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 11018 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code, commissioner's examination and duty to issue a public report
citations.quote: The Real Estate Commissioner shall make an examination of any subdivision, and shall, unless there are grounds for denial, issue to the subdivider a public report authorizing the sale or lease in this state of the lots or parcels within the subdivision.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 11018(a)-(i) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code, the nine enumerated grounds for denial of a public report
citations.quote: The grounds for denial are:(a) Failure to comply with any of the provisions in this chapter or the regulations of the commissioner pertaining thereto.(b) The sale or lease would constitute misrepresentation to or deceit or fraud of the purchasers or lessees.(c) Inability to deliver title or other interest contracted for.(d) Inability to demonstrate that adequate financial arrangements have been made for all offsite improvements included in the offering.(e) Inability to demonstrate that adequate financial arrangements have been made for any community, recreational or other facilities included in the offering. (f) Failure to make a showing that the parcels can be used for the purpose for which they are offered; and in the case of a subdivision being offered for residential purposes failure to make a showing that vehicular access and a source of potable domestic water either is available or will be available.(g) Failure to provide in the contract or other writing the use or uses for which the parcels are offered, together with any covenants or conditions relative thereto.(h) Agreements or bylaws to provide for management or other services pertaining to common facilities in the offering, which fail to comply with the regulations of the commissioner.(i) Failure to demonstrate that adequate financial arrangements have been made for any guaranty or warranty included in the offering.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause states the examination process and the nine enumerated denial grounds themselves; it does not address the separate procedures for amending, renewing, or suspending a public report once issued, does not address the commissioner's investigative or subpoena powers, and does not determine whether any specific ground for denial applies to a particular subdivision — that depends on facts about that offering's title, financing, and contract terms that this information sheet does not supply. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual grounds California's regulator applies — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific offering, or that every state's real-estate regulator reviews subdivision offerings against the same criteria.

expectedJSON.body: Bus. & Prof. Code § 11018.1(a)-(b) imposes two distinct delivery obligations once a public report has been issued. First, the owner, subdivider, or agent must give a copy of the public report to the prospective purchaser before the purchaser executes a binding contract or agreement for the sale or lease of any lot or parcel — an obligation that extends to lots or parcels the subdivider offers after repossession — and must take a receipt from the prospective purchaser in the form the Real Estate Commissioner's regulations specify. Second, separately from that purchaser-specific delivery obligation, the owner, subdivider, or agent must give a copy of the public report to any member of the public, at any time, on oral or written request, and must post a copy of the report, with a statement that a copy is available on request, in a conspicuous place at any office where sales, leases, or offers to sell or lease lots in the subdivision are regularly made.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 11018.1(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code, requirement to deliver the public report before a binding contract
citations.quote: (a) A copy of the public report of the commissioner, when issued, shall be given to the prospective purchaser by the owner, subdivider, or agent prior to the execution of a binding contract or agreement for the sale or lease of any lot or parcel in a subdivision. The requirement of this section extends to lots or parcels offered by the subdivider after repossession. A receipt shall be taken from the prospective purchaser in a form and manner as set forth in regulations of the Real Estate Commissioner.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 11018.1(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code, requirement to make the public report available to the public and post it
citations.quote: (b) A copy of the public report shall be given by the owner, subdivider, or agent at any time, upon oral or written request, to any member of the public. A copy of the public report and a statement advising that a copy of the public report may be obtained from the owner, subdivider or agent at any time, upon oral or written request, shall be posted in a conspicuous place at any office where sales or leases or offers to sell or lease lots within the subdivision are regularly made.

This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own delivery mechanism — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific offering.

expectedJSON.body: Bus. & Prof. Code § 11018.1(c) layers an additional requirement onto the public-report delivery obligation described in the preceding clause, specifically for subdivisions that are common interest developments as defined in Civil Code § 4100. At the same time the public report must be given under subdivision (a), the owner, subdivider, or agent must also give the prospective purchaser a copy of a statutory "Common Interest Development General Information" statement — prescribed statutory text describing, among other things, that the project is a common interest development, that ownership carries mandatory association membership and assessment obligations, and that governing documents (a Declaration of Restrictions/CC&Rs, articles of incorporation, and bylaws) control the purchaser's rights. The statute separately provides that failing to give this particular statement is not treated as a violation subject to Bus. & Prof. Code § 10185, a different statutory enforcement provision.
